prompt: Marketing has a dual goal. Is each move mainly about attracting new customers or keeping current ones?

cards.text: A gym offers a free first month to people who have never trained there.
cards.explanation: It reaches people who are not yet customers by promising superior value.

cards.text: A phone carrier's ads promise the fastest network to people with a rival plan.
cards.explanation: Promising superior value to win customers away from rivals attracts new customers.

cards.text: A bakery has a regular's usual order ready before she reaches the counter.
cards.explanation: Delivering satisfaction to someone who already buys keeps current customers.

cards.text: An airline rebooks a frequent flyer within minutes after a cancelled flight.
cards.explanation: Satisfying an existing customer when something goes wrong keeps them.

cards.text: A new grocery store mails opening-week deals to every home in the area.
cards.explanation: The store has no customers yet, so it promises value to attract new ones.

cards.text: A bike shop tunes up bikes it sold last year at no charge each spring.
cards.explanation: It keeps past buyers satisfied, so they stay customers.

prompt: Which philosophy is each manager following: the Production Concept or the Product Concept?

cards.text: A bike maker automates its plant so it can sell the same bike for less.
cards.explanation: Lower cost through production efficiency makes the product highly affordable.

cards.text: A phone maker adds a better camera and a faster chip every single year.
cards.explanation: Continuous improvement of performance and features is the Product Concept.

cards.text: A snack company opens more warehouses so its chips reach every corner store.
cards.explanation: Making the product available everywhere is distribution efficiency.

cards.text: A vacuum maker spends its budget making each model's suction stronger.
cards.explanation: The focus is on product quality and performance.

cards.text: A furniture firm cuts its models to three so it can build them faster and cheaper.
cards.explanation: Fewer models make production more efficient and the furniture more affordable.

cards.text: A boot maker keeps testing new materials to make the warmest boot on the market.
cards.explanation: Chasing the most quality and innovative features is the Product Concept.

prompt: You have now met four philosophies. Which one is each company following?

cases.text: A car dealer has too many of last year's models, so it doubles commissions and runs ads all weekend to move them.
cases.explanation: It starts from the factory's existing products and aims for volume through heavy selling. That is the inside-out Selling Concept.

cases.text: Before designing a stroller, a company spends months with city parents to learn what they struggle with.
cases.explanation: It starts with a well-defined market and its needs. That is the outside-in Marketing Concept.

cases.text: A shoe maker moves to a larger plant so it can cut its price and stock every discount store.
cases.explanation: Affordability and availability through production and distribution efficiency is the Production Concept.

cases.text: A blender brand adds a more powerful motor and two new settings to every model this year.
cases.explanation: Continuous product improvement in performance and features is the Product Concept.

cases.text: A gym with empty memberships to fill hires a call centre to phone every number in the area.
cases.explanation: It pushes what it already has through a large-scale selling effort.

cases.text: A bank studies how students handle money, then builds an account and app around what they told it.
cases.explanation: It learns the needs of a target market first and delivers satisfaction better than competitors.

prompt: A fast-food chain is planning a new menu the societal way. Which of the three considerations does each point serve?

cards.text: Each new item has to earn a healthy margin.
cards.explanation: The company still needs the menu to make money.

cards.text: Customers want meals that taste great and come fast.
cards.explanation: This is what consumers want in the short run.

cards.text: Every box and cup must be recyclable.
cards.explanation: Less waste serves society's well-being.

cards.text: The menu should raise sales in every store.
cards.explanation: Sales that lead to profit serve the company.

cards.text: Diners asked for bigger combo meals.
cards.explanation: It is a consumer want, which may conflict with long-run welfare.

cards.text: Salt and sugar are cut across the menu.
cards.explanation: Protecting long-run consumer health serves the public interest.

prompt: Is each case a need, a want, or a demand?

cards.text: Feeling cold on the walk to class in January
cards.explanation: A state of felt deprivation: the basic physical need for warmth.

cards.text: Feeling lonely in the first week at a new school
cards.explanation: A social need for belonging and affection.

cards.text: Wishing for the same parka everyone on campus wears
cards.explanation: The need for warmth has taken a form shaped by culture and personality.

cards.text: Craving a poutine when hungry late at night
cards.explanation: Hunger is the need. Poutine is the form it takes here, shaped by culture.

cards.text: Having saved $1,200 to buy the laptop she has picked out
cards.explanation: The want is backed by buying power, so it is a demand.

cards.text: Buying two concert tickets the moment they go on sale
cards.explanation: A want accompanied by purchasing ability is a demand.

prompt: Compare what each customer expected with how the offering performed. Is the customer dissatisfied, satisfied or delighted?

cards.text: The app promised pizza in 30 minutes. It came after an hour, cold.
cards.explanation: Performance fell short of expectations.

cards.text: She booked a basic room and was upgraded to a suite with a view.
cards.explanation: Performance exceeded expectations.

cards.text: He asked for his usual haircut and got exactly his usual haircut.
cards.explanation: Performance matched expectations.

cards.text: The ad said the earbuds last 8 hours. They die after 3.
cards.explanation: Perceived performance fell short of what the buyer expected.

cards.text: The bus was due at 8:10 and arrived at 8:10.
cards.explanation: Performance matched expectations.

cards.text: The garage quoted two days, fixed the car in two hours and washed it too.
cards.explanation: Performance went well beyond expectations.

prompt: Two graduates open a café beside campus. Put their moves in the order of the five-step marketing process.

steps.text: They talk to students between classes about what they want from a morning coffee.
steps.explanation: Step 1: understand the marketplace and customer needs and wants.

steps.text: They decide to serve students and promise good coffee that is fast and cheap.
steps.explanation: Step 2: design a customer-value-driven marketing strategy.

steps.text: They set the menu and prices, sign a lease by the main gate and launch an Instagram account.
steps.explanation: Step 3: construct an integrated marketing program that delivers superior value.

steps.text: They learn regulars' names, run a loyalty card and surprise students with free cookies in exam week.
steps.explanation: Step 4: engage customers, build profitable relationships and create customer delight.

steps.text: Loyal regulars bring steady profits, year after year.
steps.explanation: Step 5: capture value from customers to create profits and customer equity.

prompt: A new sneaker brand is designing its strategy. Which decision is each move: segmentation, targeting or the value proposition?

cases.text: The team divides sneaker buyers into runners, skaters, collectors and people who want comfort at work.
cases.explanation: Dividing the market into groups is market segmentation.

cases.text: They decide to sell only to serious runners.
cases.explanation: Selecting which segment to enter is targeting.

cases.text: They promise runners the lightest shoe that still lasts 1,000 km.
cases.explanation: The set of benefits the brand promises to deliver is its value proposition.

cases.text: They sort runners by age and by how many kilometres they run each week.
cases.explanation: Splitting the market into groups is still segmentation.

cases.text: They choose not to chase collectors, even though that group spends a lot.
cases.explanation: Deciding which segments to enter, and which to leave, is targeting.

cases.text: Their ads give runners one reason to pick them over big rivals: fewer injuries.
cases.explanation: A value proposition differentiates the brand and gives customers a compelling reason to choose it.

prompt: CRM involves acquiring, engaging, keeping and growing customers. Match each part to what a streaming service does.

pairs.match: Offers a free first month to people who have never subscribed.
pairs.explanation: Bringing in someone who is not yet a customer is acquiring.

pairs.match: Invites subscribers to vote on which cancelled show comes back.
pairs.explanation: Involving customers directly in shaping the brand is engaging.

pairs.match: Offers a cheaper plan to subscribers who click Cancel.
pairs.explanation: Holding on to a customer who is about to leave is keeping.

pairs.match: Sells current subscribers an add-on with live sports.
pairs.explanation: Selling more to a customer the firm already has is growing.

question_text: A shopper who has bought groceries at the same store every week for years switches to a rival. According to the lecture, what has the store lost?

options.option_text: Only the value of that shopper's next weekly grocery purchase.
options.option_explanation: Losing a customer means losing more than a single sale.

options.option_text: The entire future income stream that customer represented.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Customer Lifetime Value is the whole stream of purchases, so losing the customer loses that future stream.

options.option_text: Nothing lasting, because share of customer stays the same.
options.option_explanation: Share of customer is the portion of the customer's purchasing the company gets. When the shopper leaves, it falls.

options.option_text: A single sale, since each weekly purchase is a separate event.
options.option_explanation: The lecture treats purchases as a stream over a lifetime of patronage, not as separate events.

prompt: Place each customer by potential profitability and projected loyalty. Which group are they?

cases.text: A business traveller spends big on hotel stays but books whichever chain is cheapest that week.
cases.explanation: High potential profitability, low projected loyalty: a butterfly.

cases.text: A tourist buys one bottle of water at a corner store and will never pass by again.
cases.explanation: Low potential profitability and low projected loyalty: a stranger.

cases.text: A family of five does its full weekly shop at the same grocer and has for ten years.
cases.explanation: High potential profitability and high projected loyalty: a true friend.

cases.text: A client has banked with the same branch for 30 years but keeps only $40 there and calls weekly for help.
cases.explanation: High projected loyalty but low potential profitability: a barnacle.

cases.text: A regular buys a new premium bike from the same shop every two years and brings it there for every repair.
cases.explanation: Profitable and loyal: a true friend.

cases.text: A shopper visits only on clearance days, buys one cheap item and tries a different store next time.
cases.explanation: Little profit and little loyalty: a stranger.
